newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand battles finance sector problems.
newsitem.headline: Thailand battles finance sector problems.

text.p: Thailand battled to overcome a crisis of confidence in its troubled finance sector on Thursday as nervous investors made further hefty withdrawals from ailing financial institutions, analysts said.
A central bank official estimated investors withdrew close to 15 billion baht ($577 million) on Tuesday and Wednesday from 10 troubled and other financial institutions.
Already jittery markets tumbled again on Thursday on poor prospects for finance company earnings and rumours that the governor of the central bank might have to resign.
Stocks were hammered for a fourth consecutive day, closing at their lowest level in nearly five years.
Vickers Ballas research said in a report Thai Farmers Bank Plc and Bangkok Bank Plc would be the only top Thai banks to see earnings growth this year.
Further selling pressure in bank, finance and securities stocks would continue in the short-term, it said.

The Thai baht was also hammered early on Thursday after rumours the central bank governor Rerngchai Marakanond might resign. The currency, which slumped to 25.960/25.970 to the dollar in early trade, later recovered to 25.950/25.953 after the rumours were officialy denied.

"There is a confidence crisis now, people want to be assured problems in finance have been contained, that decisive leadership is there and the authorities know what to do to control the situation," said the head of a foreign brokerage, who declined to be named.
On Monday, the authorities shook up the finance sector by ordering 10 finance firms facing liquidity problems to boost their capital by a total of 8.25 billion baht ($317 million).
They also told banks and finance companies to raise provisions for bad loans, primarily to the depressed property sector, to 115 and 120 percent respectively from 100 percent.
Thai financial institutions would be required to set aside a total of 50 billion baht in additional provisions, the Bank of Thailand said.
The revamp sent shockwaves through the system.

"I see this as a scramble for safety more than a crisis of confidence. Those who are running for cover now will be the same people who will come back when everything improves," said Firdosh Bathena, senior vice-president at Asian Credit Plc.
"It's a question of let me protect my capital now and earn interest later. These problems stem from structural problems that bankers knew about all along. It will take some time to settle," he added.
Brokers said the order which was imposed by the central bank on Monday had worried investors as they believed it would affect liquidity of finance firms.
After nearly a decade of heady 9.0 percent annual average economic growth until 1995, the Thai economy grew only 6.7 percent in 1996.

Analysts expect growth this year to fall well below the 6.8 percent official forecast, especially after nearly 100 billion baht in spending cuts were ordered by the government last month, and amid the current finance sector problems and slow exports.

Officials from Moody's Investor Service are in Bangkok this week to assess whether or not to downgrade Thailand's long-term credit rating. The agency said last month it had put Thailand under review for a rating downgrade.
Thai finance firms have been hit by poor quality loan assets and a liquidity crunch due to high interest rates used by the central bank to deter speculators in the baht.
Pongsathorn Siriyothin, a spokesman for Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, said there was no conflict within the government over current economic initiatives.
"He (Amnuay) is not under any pressure. He has the prime minister's full support," he said.

The SET index finished 7.07 points lower on Thursday at 676.65 on moderate trade of about five billion baht turnover. It was the lowest close since May 19, 1992, when the index finished at 667.84. The SET-50 index ended 0.52 point down at 49.38.

"No positive news was seen in the market at all today. Investors were still shocked with a new government measures requiring commercial banks and finance firms to raise provisions for sub-standard assets," said a broker at Securities One.
